title: continuous-batching-scheduler-tuning-experiments-12
content:
Summary:
This doc collects the most recent continuous-batching scheduler tuning experiments (Nov 2025 -> Feb 2026). Goal: characterize how max_batch_size, batching_timeout_ms, and fairness policies affect latency (P50/P95/P99), throughput (tokens/s), and cold/warm tail behavior across representative workloads. Focused on our v2 scheduler with KV-cache-aware fast path enabled.

Quick conclusions / recommendations (TL;DR):
- For interactive-low-latency workloads (web chat, agents): set max_batch_size=8-16, batching_timeout_ms=5-10, fairness=per-model weighted round-robin with tenant soft-priority. This gives P95 < 120ms for 1kB prompt distribution and keeps cost reasonable.
- For throughput-heavy batch inference (async embeddings, long completions): set max_batch_size=64-128, batching_timeout_ms=20-50, fairness=throughput-first (allow larger batches). Expect 2-3x throughput (tokens/s) vs conservative settings but P99 increases significantly.
- Adaptive timeout (timeout scaled to current qlen and per-req latency budget) provides best end-to-end tradeoff; prototype reduced cost by ~12% while keeping P95 within SLOs.
- Fairness policies matter for tail latency: strict FIFO starves small requests behind large ones; weighted policies reduce P99 for small/interactive requests by up to 40%.

Experiment setup (short):
- Cluster: 4x A100 80GB (nvlink), CUDA 12.1, triton backend disabled, runtime:v2.4.3-experimental
- Models: small-medium LLMs used in experiments: redwood-3B, rw-m-7b (fp16), rw-m-13b-q4 (quantized).
- Workloads:
  * interactive-chat: arrival Poisson lambda tuned to target 50-70% GPU util, prompt distribution: median 250 tokens, 99th 1,200 tokens
  * long-generation: arrival bursty (peaks), prompt median 600 tokens, generation up to 2,048 tokens
  * embeddings: many short prompts (avg 20 tokens) high QPS
- Measurement windows: 10m warmup + 30m stable window per experiment. Metrics captured: request latency (P50/P90/P95/P99), tokens/s, GPU utilization, batching efficiency (avg batch occupancy), queue length distribution, KV-cache hit ratio.

Configurations tested (selected):
- C1 (baseline conservative): max_batch_size=32, batching_timeout_ms=40, fairness=FIFO
- C2 (low-latency): max_batch_size=8, batching_timeout_ms=8, fairness=per-model weighted RR
- C3 (throughput): max_batch_size=128, batching_timeout_ms=40, fairness=throughput-first
- C4 (adaptive): max_batch_size=64, batching_timeout_ms adaptive (min=5, max=50, scale=f(qlen,latency_budget)), fairness=weighted RR
- C5 (small-request prioritization): same as C1 but small-request fast-path enabled + per-tenant small-queue priority

Observed results (representative numbers from stable window):
1) interactive-chat workload (rw-m-7b fp16, 50% GPU util target)
- C1: P50=62ms, P95=205ms, P99=412ms, tokens/s=18k, avg batch occ=21/32
- C2: P50=48ms, P95=110ms, P99=260ms, tokens/s=13k, avg batch occ=6/8
- C3: P50=180ms, P95=540ms, P99=980ms, tokens/s=45k, avg batch occ=112/128 (note: memory pressure triggered occasional spill to CPU path)
- C4: P50=55ms, P95=130ms, P99=300ms, tokens/s=23k, avg batch occ=36/64
- C5: P50=58ms, P95=125ms, P99=210ms, tokens/s=20k, avg batch occ=20/32

Notes: C2 (low-latency) reduces P95 dramatically but throughput drops ~28% vs baseline. C4 adaptive recovers some throughput while keeping latency near low-latency targets. C5 with small-request prioritization achieves best P99 without huge throughput loss.

2) embeddings workload (many short requests, high QPS)
- C1: P50=12ms, P95=45ms, P99=110ms, tokens/s=60k, avg batch occ=25/32
- C2: P50=10ms, P95=28ms, P99=70ms, tokens/s=42k, avg batch occ=7/8
- C3: P50=20ms, P95=60ms, P99=150ms, tokens/s=120k, avg batch occ=96/128
- C4: P50=11ms, P95=30ms, P99=85ms, tokens/s=78k, avg batch occ=44/64

Notes: For very short work, larger batches improve tokens/s significantly; however if requests are latency-sensitive, moderate batch sizes + small timeout wins.

3) long-generation workload (large outputs)
- C1: P50=210ms, P95=770ms, P99=1.9s, tokens/s=9k, avg batch occ=14/32
- C2: P50=190ms, P95=610ms, P99=1.5s, tokens/s=7k, avg batch occ=7/8
- C3: P50=450ms, P95=1.3s, P99=3.8s, tokens/s=25k, avg batch occ=98/128
- C4: P50=220ms, P95=700ms, P99=1.6s, tokens/s=12k, avg batch occ=52/64

Profiling & bottlenecks observed:
- Kernel-level: attention kernel scales well with batch size for long sequences; however smaller sequences have higher per-token overhead due to launch overheads.
- Scheduler: contention in the request-coordinator lock observed when qlen spikes > 500; this manifests as extra queuing latency and occasional batch creation delays.
- KV-cache interaction: when KV-cache hit ratio is high, batching more aggressively provides diminishing returns since kb cache reuse (fast-path) already reduces compute; but if we batch across requests with different prefixes we lose cache locality -> tail latency spikes.
- Memory pressure: extremely large batches on quantized models occasionally trigger temporary memory oversubscription on GPU leading to device fallback and large P99 spikes. We saw this in C3 with rw-m-13b-q4 under bursty arrivals.

Fairness experiments (impact on small/interactive requests):
- FIFO: simple but favors large requests that arrived earlier; observed small-request starvation when mixed workloads present. P99 for small requests up to 2.5x worse.
- Weighted round-robin (per-model weights + tenant soft-priority): reduces small-request P99 by ~35% vs FIFO while keeping overall throughput within 90% of FIFO in most cases.
- Strict priority (small requests always prioritized): best small-request latency but decreases throughput of long-running batches and increases average latency for background jobs; can be used for tight SLAs but must be limited by leased capacity.

Adaptive timeout prototype details:
- Heuristic used: timeout = clamp(base + alpha * sqrt(qlen), min, max) but scaled down when KV-cache hit ratio > 0.7
- Observed behavior: under steady QPS, adaptive timeout settled near 12-20ms for interactive workload, which allowed batches to reach 30-40% occupancy without adding >20ms extra P95.
- Implementation notes: requires low-overhead qlen sampler (used eBPF in prototype) and per-scheduler moving average; we need to instrument more metrics before rollout.

Action items / next steps:
1) Short term (2-4 weeks):
  - Add per-tenant small-request fast-path (implements C5 semantics) behind a feature flag. Owner: Rohit. Jira: JIRA-ENG-1289.
  - Improve request-coordinator lock contention by sharding queue into N stripes (experiment with N=8). Owner: Samira.
  - Roll out adaptive timeout canary on ~5% of production traffic for interactive model family. Owner: Emily.

2) Medium term (1-3 months):
  - Add kernel-level metrics and finer-grained cache-locality telemetry to correlate batch composition with KV-cache hit ratio. Owner: Luca.
  - Implement batch-size caps per-model and per-tenant automatically based on profile (model-optimal batch size heuristics).
  - Formalize fairness policies in config UI: weighted RR, strict priority, and SLA-backed reserved slots.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to automatically classify "small/interactive" vs "large/background" requests at ingress without adding a required field from customers? We have heuristics but they misclassify ~8% of cases.
- Should we expose adaptive timeout knobs to customers or keep as opaque server-side optimization? (product decision + security implications).
- Need to reproduce memory-fallback case under quantized models in a deterministic test harness (ticket assigned).

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers above are from matrics aggregated across 30m windows and are intended as directional guidance; per-model tuning will be required.
- See linked artifacts for raw CSVs and flamegraphs (Confluence page).
- This doc supersedes experiment-11; keep that file for traceability.
